en: Articular cartilage — acromioclavicular joint, clavicle surface
plain: The smooth glassy layer capping the clavicle where it forms the acromioclavicular joint. It lets the two bones slide against each other almost without friction.

plain: The long bone of the palm leading to the index finger.

plain: The long bone of the palm leading to the middle finger.
detail: Carries a styloid process on its base; also fixed, forming the stable central pillar of the hand with the 2nd.

plain: The long bone of the palm leading to the ring finger.
detail: More mobile than the 2nd and 3rd, allowing the palm to cup.

plain: The long bone of the foot leading to the great toe.
detail: The shortest and thickest metatarsal. It carries the most weight of the forefoot, and two sesamoid bones sit beneath its head.

plain: The long bone of the foot leading to the 2nd toe.
detail: The longest metatarsal, wedged firmly between the cuneiforms — the keystone of the transverse arch and the commonest site of a march (stress) fracture.

plain: The long bone of the foot leading to the 3rd toe.
detail: A slender middle metatarsal contributing to the transverse arch.

plain: The long bone of the foot leading to the 4th toe.
detail: Articulates with the cuboid, giving it more mobility than the medial three.

plain: The long bone of the foot leading to the little toe.
detail: Carries the prominent tuberosity on its base for fibularis brevis — the classic avulsion fracture site in an inversion injury.

plain: The middle of the three bones of the 2nd toe, between the proximal and distal phalanges.

plain: A muscle that pulls the great toe away from the others.

plain: A muscle that pulls the knee's suprapatellar bursa upwards so it is not pinched.
detail: From the lower anterior femur to the suprapatellar bursa. Supplied by the femoral nerve.

plain: A muscle that cocks the wrist back and tilts it towards the little finger.
detail: From the lateral epicondyle and the posterior ulna to the base of the 5th metacarpal. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

plain: A muscle that straightens the four fingers.
detail: From the common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle to the extensor expansions of the four fingers. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
clinical: Its tendons are connected on the back of the hand by intertendinous bands, which is why the ring finger cannot be extended fully on its own.

plain: A muscle that helps lift the toes, from within the foot itself.
detail: From the upper lateral surface of the calcaneus to the extensor expansions of the medial four toes. Supplied by the deep fibular nerve.
meshNames: Extensor digitorum brevis origin and insertion.r
clinical: Its fleshy belly on the outer side of the foot is often mistaken for swelling.

plain: A muscle that lifts the four lesser toes and helps turn the foot up.

plain: A muscle that lifts the great toe and helps turn the foot up.
detail: From the middle fibula and interosseous membrane to the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe. Supplied by the deep fibular nerve.
clinical: Its power against resistance is the standard bedside test of the L5 root.

plain: A muscle that straightens the first joint of the thumb.
detail: From the posterior radius and interosseous membrane to the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

clinical: With abductor pollicis longus it forms the front border of the anatomical snuffbox, and shares the sheath inflamed in de Quervain's tenosynovitis.

plain: A muscle that straightens the last joint of the thumb and pulls it backwards.
detail: From the posterior ulna and interosseous membrane to the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. Supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
meshNames: Extensor pollicis longus origin and insertion.r
clinical: Its tendon hooks round the dorsal tubercle of the radius, and can rupture there after a Colles fracture.

plain: A muscle that turns the sole outwards.
detail: From the lower lateral shaft of the fibula to the tuberosity at the base of the 5th metatarsal. Supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.
clinical: A sudden inversion can avulse that tuberosity — the commonest fracture of the midfoot.

plain: A muscle that turns the sole outwards and points the foot down.
detail: From the head and upper lateral shaft of the fibula to the base of the 1st metatarsal and the medial cuneiform, crossing the sole. Supplied by the superficial fibular nerve.
clinical: Because its tendon crosses the sole, it is a key support of the transverse arch.

plain: A muscle that curls the middle joints of the four lesser toes.
detail: From the medial tubercle of the calcaneus and the plantar aponeurosis to the middle phalanges of the lateral four toes. Supplied by the medial plantar nerve.
meshNames: Flexor digitorum brevis origin and insertion.r

plain: A muscle that curls the four lesser toes and helps point the foot down.
detail: From the posterior surface of the tibia below the soleal line to the bases of the distal phalanges of the lateral four toes. Supplied by the tibial nerve.
meshNames: Flexor digitorum longus origin and insertion.r
clinical: Its tendon crosses that of flexor hallucis longus in the sole at the 'knot of Henry'.

plain: A muscle that bends the last joint of the thumb.
detail: From the anterior surface of the radius and the interosseous membrane to the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. Supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve.
meshNames: Flexor pollicis longus origin and insertion.r
clinical: The only muscle that can flex the thumb's interphalangeal joint — which is why that joint flexes to compensate in Froment's sign.

plain: A muscle that swings the thumb across the palm to meet the other fingers.
detail: From the flexor retinaculum and the tubercle of the trapezium to the whole lateral border of the 1st metacarpal. Supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.
clinical: Opposition is the movement lost first and most obviously in carpal tunnel syndrome.

plain: A muscle that tenses the palmar skin and helps bend the wrist.
detail: From the medial epicondyle by the common flexor origin to the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. Supplied by the median nerve.
clinical: Absent in about 15 per cent of people, and expendable — which makes it the standard donor tendon for grafting.

plain: A muscle that pulls the thigh inwards and forwards.
detail: From the pecten of the pubis to the pectineal line of the femur. Supplied by the femoral nerve, sometimes with the obturator.
clinical: Forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle.

plain: A muscle that assists the calf weakly in pointing the foot down.
detail: From the lateral supracondylar line of the femur to the calcaneal tendon or the calcaneus. Supplied by the tibial nerve.
clinical: A long thin tendon, absent in about a tenth of people, and often harvested for grafting.

plain: A muscle that turns the palm downwards.
detail: From the lower quarter of the anterior ulna to the lower quarter of the anterior radius. Supplied by the anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve.
clinical: The deepest muscle of the front of the forearm, and the primary pronator in unresisted movement.

plain: A muscle that turns the thigh outwards.
detail: From the lateral border of the ischial tuberosity to the quadrate tubercle of the femur. Supplied by the nerve to quadratus femoris.

plain: A muscle that corrects the pull of the long toe flexor so the toes bend straight.
detail: From the plantar surface of the calcaneus to the tendon of flexor digitorum longus. Supplied by the lateral plantar nerve.

plain: The soft gel at the centre of an intervertebral disc. It behaves like a water cushion, spreading load evenly across the vertebra below.
detail: A remnant of the embryonic notochord, about 80 per cent water in youth. It is held under pressure by the anulus fibrosus around it, and dries out with age, which is why we lose height through the day and over a lifetime.
clinical: If the anulus tears, the nucleus can herniate — usually posterolaterally, where the posterior longitudinal ligament is narrowest — and press on the nerve root, causing sciatica.

plain: The joint surface where the head of this rib meets the bodies of the vertebrae, letting the rib swing as you breathe.
detail: A typical rib head carries two facets and articulates with its own vertebra and the one above, across the intervertebral disc.
clinical: Together these two joints fix the axis about which the rib rotates — pump-handle above, raising the sternum, and bucket-handle below, widening the chest.

plain: The joint surface where the tubercle of this rib meets the transverse process of its vertebra.
detail: The costotransverse joint. In the upper ribs its surface is curved, producing a pump-handle movement; lower down it is flatter, giving a bucket-handle movement.
clinical: Together these two joints fix the axis about which the rib rotates — pump-handle above, raising the sternum, and bucket-handle below, widening the chest.

plain: A neck vertebra. Every cervical vertebra has a hole in each side process that no other vertebra has — the artery to the brain passes up through them.
detail: Small body, triangular vertebral foramen, and a foramen transversarium in each transverse process. C3 to C6 have bifid spines; C7 has a long single spine you can feel.
clinical: The vertebral artery ascends through the foramina transversaria of C6 up to C1. C7's prominent spine is the landmark for counting vertebral levels.

plain: A lower back vertebra. These carry the most weight, so their bodies are the largest of all.
detail: Massive kidney-shaped body, no costal facets and no foramen transversarium, a short blunt spine, and sagittally set facet joints that allow flexion and extension but little rotation.
clinical: The highest points of the iliac crests lie at L4, guiding lumbar puncture at L3/L4 or L4/L5 — safely below the conus medullaris, which ends around L1/L2 in adults.

plain: A chest vertebra. These are the only vertebrae with ribs attached, and their spines slope steeply downwards like roof tiles.
detail: Costal facets on the body for the rib head and on the transverse process for the rib tubercle, a circular vertebral foramen, and a long downward-sloping spine.
clinical: The spines overlap so steeply that the tip of a mid-thoracic spine lies level with the body of the vertebra below — which matters when localising a level from the surface.
